sections.title: Understanding Terrorism and Extremism: Islamic Perspective
sections.body: Islam forbids deliberate attacks on innocent people. The Quran treats the unlawful killing of one person as an offense against all humanity, and Islamic law permits fighting only in defined circumstances while forbidding transgression. Terrorism that targets civilians therefore contradicts Islamic scripture, the Prophet's example, and the central duty to protect life.

sections.title: The Sanctity of Human Life: Islam's Foundational Principle
sections.body:
At the heart of Islamic teaching on violence lies a principle of profound simplicity: human life is sacred. The Quran articulates this principle with striking force through the story of the sons of Adam. The verse states that whoever kills a soul unlawfully—except in just retaliation or to prevent corruption on earth—is as if he has killed all of humanity; and whoever saves a life is as if he has saved all of humanity. This teaching establishes that a single human life possesses worth equivalent to the entire human species. Consequently, the taking of even one innocent life is treated as a cosmic transgression, not merely a crime against an individual but an offense against the whole of creation.

This principle appears early in Islamic revelation during the Medinan period when Muslim society was establishing legal foundations. The verse does not emerge from an abstract theological exercise but from the concrete question: how should a believing community treat human life? The answer provided is unambiguous. No single person, regardless of their station or wealth or authority, may decide to terminate human life except under the most severe and restricted circumstances.

The principle extends beyond a mere prohibition. The second half of the verse—that saving one life equals saving humanity—inverts the moral calculus. This is not merely about restraint from harm but about the positive duty to preserve and protect life. A Muslim scholar or judge who works to preserve justice and prevent bloodshed participates in the act of saving all humanity. The entire legal framework of Islamic jurisprudence regarding violence emerges from this foundational conviction about the absolute value of human life.

sections.title: Explicit Prohibitions on Killing in Islamic Law
sections.body:
Beyond the principle of human life's sanctity, Islamic scripture contains explicit prohibitions against killing oneself or one another. The Quran directly commands believers: "Do not kill yourselves [or one another]." This prohibition is presented within the context of commandments about consuming wealth lawfully and conducting commerce with mutual consent. The juxtaposition is deliberate: believers are instructed not to consume one another's property unlawfully and not to kill one another. Both theft and murder are violations of property rights and bodily integrity, violations of the covenant between community members.

The verse continues: "Indeed, Allah is to you ever Merciful." This framing is crucial. The prohibition on killing is not merely a legal rule to be obeyed from fear; it is rooted in divine mercy. God's prohibition is understood as an act of kindness and protection toward the Muslim community. Islamic jurisprudence has historically interpreted this verse to mean that Muslims have a collective responsibility to preserve the sanctity of life within their community and toward all human beings.

Combined with the principle established in Quran 5:32, these verses create a comprehensive framework. Killing is prohibited except in extremely limited circumstances: legitimate self-defense, legal punishment following due process for grave crimes, and lawful warfare under defined authority and limits. Outside these narrow exceptions, all killing is forbidden. There is no Islamic sanction for vigilante violence, honor killing, or killing for political, ideological, or religious reasons outside these defined legal channels.

Islamic legal scholars across centuries have elaborated on these prohibitions, establishing detailed rules for the lawful use of force. These rules require legitimate authority, just cause, proportional response, and protection of noncombatants. A private individual or militia cannot simply declare themselves at war and begin taking lives. The restrictions are extensive precisely because Islamic law treats the taking of life as the most serious possible transgression against creation.

sections.title: Classical Rules of Warfare and the Modern Defensive-War Position
sections.body:
Quran 2:190 commands fighting those who fight while forbidding transgression. Modern Muslim writers frequently build a defensive theory of war from this verse, Quran 22:39-40, treaty obligations, and the protection of noncombatants. That is an important contemporary position, but it should not be projected backward as the only doctrine in classical law.

Classical Sunni jurists agreed that private persons could not simply declare unrestricted violence and that warfare belonged to public authority. They developed rules governing treaties, safe-conduct, protected persons, property, and categories of combatants. They nevertheless differed over the grounds and aims of jihad, and major premodern schools allowed forms of state-led offensive warfare under conditions that modern defensive-only theories reject or reinterpret.

This historical complexity does not provide a defense of terrorism. Secret or non-state attacks deliberately directed at civilians do not become lawful because classical jurists discussed offensive war between polities. The relevant modern judgment must distinguish jus ad bellum questions, conduct during war, rebellion, banditry, murder, and terrorism rather than treating them as one category.

Claims of consensus should therefore be narrow: contemporary Muslim institutions overwhelmingly condemn intentional attacks on civilians, while the broader history of Islamic war law contains genuine disagreements that must be acknowledged.

sections.title: Obligations Toward Non-Combatants and Peacemakers
sections.body:
Islamic jurisprudence extends beyond defining when force is permissible to establishing how Muslims should treat those who are not engaged in hostilities. A Quranic verse states: "Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly."

This verse is remarkable in its scope. It establishes that Muslims have a positive obligation of kindness and justice toward people of other faiths, as long as those people are not engaged in active warfare against Muslims or driving them from their homes. The teaching is not about merely tolerating non-Muslims but about actively showing them righteousness and justice. The verse concludes that God loves those who are just. This is a powerful statement: the divine preference is for Muslims to maintain ethical standards even toward those outside their religious community.

The verse implicitly recognizes categories of people: those actively fighting, those who have oppressed Muslims, and those simply living peacefully. The obligations shift depending on which category applies. But for the vast majority of people—those who are not militarily engaged—the Islamic duty is toward justice and kindness. This principle has profound implications for how Islamic law approaches terrorism. Most victims of terrorist attacks are innocent civilians, whether Muslim or non-Muslim, who have not fought Muslims or expelled them from their homes. By the logic of this verse, Islamic law mandates that such people should be treated with justice and kindness, not targeted for violence.

The tradition also praises gentleness without inventing a rule in the Prophet's name. Sahih Muslim 2594a reports: 'Gentleness is not found in anything except that it beautifies it, and it is not withdrawn from anything except that it makes it defective.' This ethical preference supports reconciliation and restraint, while questions about when force is lawful still belong to the separate jurisprudence of war, policing, and self-defense.

sections.title: Mainstream Muslim Scholarly Condemnation of Terrorism
sections.body:
Mainstream Muslim scholars and institutions condemn deliberate attacks on innocent civilians. The religious basis is the Quran's prohibition on unlawful killing and transgression, reinforced by the Prophet's protection of noncombatants.

After the September 11 attacks, Yusuf al-Qaradawi, Tariq Bishri, Muhammad S. Awwa, Fahmi Huwaydi, Haytham Khayyat, and Taha Jabir al-Alwani issued a statement on September 27, 2001. It condemned terrorizing innocents and called for the perpetrators to face impartial justice. Its [archived text](https://kurzman.unc.edu/islamic-statements-against-terrorism/) addresses violence against innocents and impartial justice.

A separate [Fiqh Council of North America fatwa, dated July 28, 2005](https://afjcis.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/fatwa-against-terrorism.pdf), explicitly condemned targeting civilian life and property through suicide bombings or other attacks. Such institutional statements make the protection of civilians clear. Disputes over the historical grounds for warfare do not make civilians lawful targets, and a group's religious slogans do not create authority to kill them.

sections.title: How Terrorist Groups Misuse Islamic Texts
sections.body:
Terrorist groups often quote fighting verses without the limits around them. Quran 2:190 says, “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress,” while Quran 2:191 describes a specific conflict in which Muslims had been expelled and attacked. Removing that setting turns a restricted permission into a false license for violence.

These groups also declare private organizations to be authorities with power to wage war, redefine civilians as enemies, and ignore the rules protecting women, children, the elderly, worshippers, and other non-combatants. Their selective reading contradicts the Quran's commands of justice, protection, and peace when an enemy inclines to peace.

sections.title: Legitimate Islamic Critiques of Extremism and Terrorism
sections.body:
Islamic tradition gives Muslims internal tools for resisting extremism. The Prophet warned against excess in religion, praised mercy and restraint, and forbade treachery and the killing of non-combatants. Scholars also require lawful authority, a legitimate cause, and proportional conduct before force can be considered.

These standards expose the error of terrorist ideology: zeal does not create legal authority, anger does not make civilians lawful targets, and a claimed religious goal cannot excuse forbidden means.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Mainstream Islamic Position and Its Bases
sections.body:
Islamic scripture and law clearly condemn terrorism: deliberately targeting innocent civilians is forbidden. Quran 5:32 describes unlawful killing as an offense comparable to killing all humanity, while Quran 2:190 permits fighting those who fight Muslims and immediately forbids transgression. Prophetic instructions also prohibit killing women, children, and other non-combatants. A military operation cannot be called Islamic merely because a group invokes Allah's name; its targets, authority, purpose, and conduct must meet Islamic limits.

Mainstream Muslim scholars and institutions therefore condemn attacks on civilians as a grave sin and a violation of Islamic law. Groups that justify terrorism by isolating fighting verses ignore the passages that restrict combat, protect non-combatants, honor treaties, and command justice. Islam's prohibition is not a vague preference: the protection of innocent life is a clear religious and legal duty.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Terrorism and Extremism: Islamic Perspective
sections.body: Islam's position is clear: innocent life is sacred, deliberate attacks on civilians are forbidden, and fighting is permitted only within strict limits. Quranic commands, the Prophet's practice, and Islamic jurisprudence all support this protection. Terrorist groups violate Islam when they kill non-combatants, break treaties, or claim authority to wage violence without lawful grounds.

quranVerses.arabic: مِنْ أَجْلِ ذَٰلِكَ كَتَبْنَا عَلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنَّهُۥ مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًۢا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًۭا وَمَنْ أَحْيَاهَا فَكَأَنَّمَآ أَحْيَا ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًۭا ۚ وَلَقَدْ جَآءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُنَا بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَثِيرًۭا مِّنْهُم بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لَمُسْرِفُونَ
quranVerses.translation: Because of that, We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely. And our messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, [even] after that, throughout the land, were transgressors.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَٰلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ تِجَٰرَةً عَن تَرَاضٍۢ مِّنكُمْ ۚ وَلَا تَقْتُلُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِكُمْ رَحِيمًۭا
quranVerses.translation: O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves [or one another]. Indeed, Allah is to you ever Merciful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِنَّمَا جَزَٰٓؤُا۟ ٱلَّذِينَ يُحَارِبُونَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ وَيَسْعَوْنَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَسَادًا أَن يُقَتَّلُوٓا۟ أَوْ يُصَلَّبُوٓا۟ أَوْ تُقَطَّعَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَأَرْجُلُهُم مِّنْ خِلَٰفٍ أَوْ يُنفَوْا۟ مِنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ لَهُمْ خِزْىٌۭ فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا ۖ وَلَهُمْ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ
quranVerses.translation: Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [to cause] corruption is none but that they be killed or crucified or that their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides or that they be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment,
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ حَيْثُ ثَقِفْتُمُوهُمْ وَأَخْرِجُوهُم مِّنْ حَيْثُ أَخْرَجُوكُمْ ۚ وَٱلْفِتْنَةُ أَشَدُّ مِنَ ٱلْقَتْلِ ۚ وَلَا تُقَٰتِلُوهُمْ عِندَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ حَتَّىٰ يُقَٰتِلُوكُمْ فِيهِ ۖ فَإِن قَٰتَلُوكُمْ فَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ ۗ كَذَٰلِكَ جَزَآءُ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ
quranVerses.translation: And kill them wherever you overtake them and expel them from wherever they have expelled you, and fitnah is worse than killing. And do not fight them at al-Masjid al- Haram until they fight you there. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: أُذِنَ لِلَّذِينَ يُقَٰتَلُونَ بِأَنَّهُمْ ظُلِمُوا۟ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ نَصْرِهِمْ لَقَدِيرٌ
quranVerses.translation: Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allah is competent to give them victory.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: يَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلشَّهْرِ ٱلْحَرَامِ قِتَالٍۢ فِيهِ ۖ قُلْ قِتَالٌۭ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌۭ ۖ وَصَدٌّ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَكُفْرٌۢ بِهِۦ وَٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ وَإِخْرَاجُ أَهْلِهِۦ مِنْهُ أَكْبَرُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ ۚ وَٱلْفِتْنَةُ أَكْبَرُ مِنَ ٱلْقَتْلِ ۗ وَلَا يَزَالُونَ يُقَٰتِلُونَكُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَرُدُّوكُمْ عَن دِينِكُمْ إِنِ ٱسْتَطَٰعُوا۟ ۚ وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكُمْ عَن دِينِهِۦ فَيَمُتْ وَهُوَ كَافِرٌۭ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ حَبِطَتْ أَعْمَٰلُهُمْ فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ ۖ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ أَصْحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِ ۖ هُمْ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ
quranVerses.translation: They ask you about the sacred month - about fighting therein. Say, "Fighting therein is great [sin], but averting [people] from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him and [preventing access to] al-Masjid al-Haram and the expulsion of its people therefrom are greater [evil] in the sight of Allah. And fitnah is greater than killing." And they will continue to fight you until they turn you back from your religion if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion [to disbelief] and dies while he is a disbeliever - for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein eternally.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: لَآ إِكْرَاهَ فِى ٱلدِّينِ ۖ قَد تَّبَيَّنَ ٱلرُّشْدُ مِنَ ٱلْغَىِّ ۚ فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بِٱلطَّٰغُوتِ وَيُؤْمِنۢ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدِ ٱسْتَمْسَكَ بِٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ لَا ٱنفِصَامَ لَهَا ۗ وَٱللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ
quranVerses.translation: There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong. So whoever disbelieves in Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold with no break in it. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: لَّا يَنْهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقَٰتِلُوكُمْ فِى ٱلدِّينِ وَلَمْ يُخْرِجُوكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمْ أَن تَبَرُّوهُمْ وَتُقْسِطُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُقْسِطِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: فَإِذَا ٱنسَلَخَ ٱلْأَشْهُرُ ٱلْحُرُمُ فَٱقْتُلُوا۟ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ وَخُذُوهُمْ وَٱحْصُرُوهُمْ وَٱقْعُدُوا۟ لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍۢ ۚ فَإِن تَابُوا۟ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتَوُا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ فَخَلُّوا۟ سَبِيلَهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ
quranVerses.translation: And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them and capture them and besiege them and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they should repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, let them [go] on their way. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَٰتِلُوا۟ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِينَ يُقَٰتِلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُعْتَدِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress. Indeed. Allah does not like transgressors.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.”

For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.

faq.question: Does Islamic law permit suicide bombing?
faq.answer: Suicide is prohibited in Islam. Deliberate attacks on innocent civilians are also prohibited, whatever weapon is used. The Fiqh Council of North America's 2005 fatwa specifically condemned targeting civilian life and property through suicide bombings or other attacks. Historical disputes over particular military operations do not justify terrorist attacks on civilians.

faq.question: What makes Islamic law prohibit terrorism specifically?
faq.answer: Islamic law protects life, forbids treachery, and restricts the use of force. Quran 5:32 describes unlawful killing as an offense comparable to killing all humanity. The Prophet forbade killing women and children. A private group's anger or religious claims create no right to wage violence against civilians. Classical jurists and contemporary scholars differ over some grounds for warfare; those debates do not remove its limits or permit terrorism.

faq.question: How do Islamic scholars respond when terrorists claim religious justification?
faq.answer: Islamic scholars emphasize that terrorist groups misuse religious texts by quoting them out of context, ignoring the conditions Islamic law places on warfare, and claiming authority they do not possess. Mainstream scholars point out that Islamic jurisprudence has developed over fourteen centuries and was refined specifically to address questions about the use of force. Terrorists are not following this jurisprudence; they are abandoning it. The overwhelming scholarly consensus explicitly condemns terrorism, and Muslims are taught to follow this consensus. Scholars also note that terrorist ideologies often contradict core Islamic principles like mercy, justice, and the value of human life.

faq.question: Is terrorism unique to Islam?
faq.answer: No. Religious and secular movements have used violence against civilians in different settings. Those examples show that terrorism is not exclusive to Muslims; they do not establish which religion has a higher rate. A comparative rate would require a defined period, population, dataset, and meaning of terrorism. Attacks committed in Islam's name should be judged against its prohibition on killing innocent people.

faq.question: What is the difference between Islamic teachings about self-defense and terrorism?
faq.answer: Self-defense, as permitted in Islamic law, requires legitimate authority, proportional response, protection of noncombatants, and response to actual aggression. It is a narrow permission granted to those being actively attacked or oppressed. Terrorism, by contrast, involves intentional targeting of civilians by non-authorities for political or ideological purposes. Terrorism seeks to spread fear and destabilize society, while self-defense aims to stop aggression. Islamic law distinguishes sharply between these categories. A private individual or group cannot decide they have been wronged and begin killing people; legitimate authority is essential. Terrorists lack such authority and intentionally target those not engaged in hostilities against them.

faq.question: How do Muslims balance religious principles with modern challenges of terrorism?
faq.answer: Muslims apply classical Islamic jurisprudence to modern circumstances. Islamic law has always required that interpretations address contemporary issues while remaining faithful to foundational principles. Modern Islamic scholars recognize that suicide bombing, targeting civilians, and uncontrolled violence by private groups are new forms of aggression that Islamic law must address clearly. The scholarly consensus is that Islamic law, properly understood, provides comprehensive condemnation of terrorism. This is not a compromise of Islamic principles but rather their faithful application. Muslims in countries affected by terrorism emphasize that their religion provides resources for condemning it, and that terrorists are betraying Islamic teaching.

furtherReading.title: Shari'ah Law: An Introduction
furtherReading.author: Mohammad Hashim Kamali
furtherReading.note: An accessible overview by a leading contemporary scholar of Islamic jurisprudence, covering the sources and methodology of Islamic law, including how classical principles are applied to modern circumstances.

furtherReading.title: War and Peace in the Law of Islam
furtherReading.author: Majid Khadduri
furtherReading.note: The classic academic study of the classical Islamic law of war and peace, including the doctrines of jihad, siyar (international law), and the treatment of combatants and noncombatants.

furtherReading.title: Unholy War: Terror in the Name of Islam
